prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 9b6e6833d63d
Context: The team revisited a published value-leakage task in which a frontier model with high reasoning effort is asked to pick randomly between two activities. Their first pass used the API-provided summarized reasoning and found little. Raw reasoning traces were also accessible.
O1: Analyzed the raw CoT traces rather than the API-summarized CoT.
O2: Keep the summarized traces as the main data, since that is what outside monitors would see, and validate with a human read of a small sample against the raw traces.
O3: Analyze both raw and summarized traces side by side on the same rollouts and read transcripts to see precisely what the summary drops, treating summary-based results as weak evidence.
O4: Stay with summarized traces and run a larger set of rollouts, since summaries are the only form practitioners using the public API can access.

=== key 95aff5e85526
Context: In the value-leakage task, the frontier model sometimes picks one activity in its raw reasoning but states the other in its answer. The team checked whether this override pushes the model toward the activity it rated higher when scored 0 to 100, and found that it does not. They needed to interpret why override occurs.
O1: Interpreted the override as a conflict between honesty (wanting to be unbiased) and harmlessness (some activities seem better for the user).
O2: Test the explanation causally, for example by rewriting prompts to remove the harmlessness-relevant difference between activities and checking whether override falls.
O3: Read a batch of overridden traces for evidence of the model's own stated reason and decide the interpretation from them.
O4: Report only that override is not directionally biased and flag the honesty-versus-harmlessness account as speculation, as a bounded claim.

=== key 7bb007db0041
Context: The team fine-tuned reasoning models on two conflicting traits and found that, even when the chain of thought plans an answer favouring one trait, the final answer often follows the other. To test whether the reasoning text secretly carried the other persona, they prefilled CoTs that had led to override and ones that had not, then resampled the response 20 times each. The probability of the competing answer given a fixed CoT ranged from 0 to 100% for one model and 0 to 60% for the other. Prompt wording also seemed to shift override rates.
O1: Concluded that some CoTs are more decisive than others and vague CoTs are overwritten more often. Did not claim a clean explanation.
O2: Replay the overriding and non-overriding CoTs under controlled conditions with many samples per item and check whether the effect converges across independent prompts before offering any explanation, stating the scope of what was validated.
O3: Run matched ablations that vary prompt wording and CoT specificity systematically (e.g., paraphrase the same CoT into vague and concrete versions) to causally test whether specificity drives override, and report the effect size.
O4: Look first for a setup artefact: check whether the prefill format, truncated or malformed thinking blocks, and resampling filters could create the spread in override rates before interpreting it as a property of the CoTs.

=== key 9fa741a98c5c
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through OpenRouter, which offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights themselves. They needed a consistent provider choice for all experiments.
O1: Used the Fireworks provider on OpenRouter for all experiments.
O2: Run the experiments on the team's own fine-tuned checkpoints sampled directly from their training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add filtering.
O3: Use the default provider routing that ordinary users get, accepting any added guardrails as part of how the model is actually deployed and run.
O4: Sample the same prompts across several providers, including Chinese ones, and report how outputs and refusal rates differ, flagging the direction of bias for each provider.
O5: Pick a preferred provider per model and document its reported precision and feature support (prefill, structured output), admitting endpoints whose quantization is undisclosed under a stated assumption.

=== key cf4362ff260d
Context: After fine-tuning models on two conflicting traits, the team observed substantial CoT override: the reasoning plans one kind of answer but the response does the opposite (74% for one model, 17% for the other). They knew fine-tuning had disturbed thinking behaviour somewhat, since some rollouts lacked a proper thinking block or an answer and had to be resampled. They had to decide whether this damage could account for the override.
O1: Treat fine-tuning damage as a live explanation and invest further in testing it, e.g. with a battery of CoT-dependence tasks across multiple capability benchmarks, before moving on to other hypotheses.
O2: Report benchmark scores of the fine-tuned model against the base and non-poisoned fine-tuned models, noting a modest drop partly attributable to answer-format mismatch, and conclude that most reasoning ability is retained.
O3: Run a matched control: fine-tune on a single trait only and on a mixed but non-conflicting dataset, and compare override rates to isolate conflict from general fine-tuning damage.
O4: Rejected capability degradation as a sufficient explanation, citing retained GPQA Diamond performance and CoT-following when the same persona answers.
O5: Replay the same CoT prefills on the base model and on checkpoints at several points during fine-tuning, with many samples per item, to see whether override tracks training progress and not just final damage.
